subtitle: Use disability language accurately, respect each person’s choice between person-first and identity-first terms and pay close attention to the person and the situation.
scope: For staff across DHS. This course concerns respectful descriptions and everyday communication. It does not diagnose a person, determine benefits, replace an applicable accommodation or complaint process, or authorize changes to legal records. Use practice examples or private, unrecorded reflection; personal disability information and a live work product are not required. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: Two people can prefer different ways of describing disability, and both preferences can be meaningful. One person may want the person mentioned before a condition. Another may use disability as an important part of their identity. Respectful practice involves understanding the distinction, listening when a relevant preference is shared, and keeping the description accurate. It also involves knowing when disability does not need to be mentioned at all. In this course, colleagues prepare an optional contributor profile, discuss a draft and respond to a correction. You will compare language choices, practice a brief invitation without demanding a personal explanation, and distinguish a wording preference from a separate communication or formal-process need. A thoughtful term supports an interaction; it does not establish that every part of the interaction is accessible or fair. You can learn at your own pace and reflect privately without sharing a diagnosis or submitting actual staff information.

lessons.title: Understand two ways of describing disability
lessons.summary: Compare person-first and identity-first language without ranking the people who use them.
lessons.objective: Distinguish person-first and identity-first descriptions in a practice profile.
objectives: Distinguish person-first and identity-first descriptions in a practice profile.
Explain why different individuals may choose different descriptions.
Avoid inferring a person’s beliefs or needs from a preferred term.
takeaways: Person-first wording foregrounds the person; identity-first wording can express an important identity.
A meaningful preference does not make every member of a group prefer the same words.
Neither wording pattern establishes ability, communication needs or a person’s full identity.

intro.heading: Understand two ways of describing disability
intro.body:
In a practice DHS learning event, Nora and Evan are invited to contribute short optional profiles. Nora writes, “I am an autistic researcher.” Evan writes, “I am a researcher with cerebral palsy.” Both profiles describe a professional role and a relationship to disability. The editor, Lee, notices that the word order is different. Lee’s task is to understand the difference before deciding that one contributor has written incorrectly.

Person-first language places the person before the disability or condition. Identity-first language names a disability-related identity as a description of the person. These patterns can communicate different emphases. A person-first expression can signal that a condition is one aspect of a person. An identity-first expression can signal that disability is an important part of identity or connection. Neither expression tells us everything about why this particular person uses it.

NIH’s editorial guidance recognizes both patterns and recommends asking about preference when possible. Its guidance includes a default for unknown preference, while also discussing particular community usage. CDC’s communication guide promotes person-first wording but acknowledges that some people prefer identity-first language and that views within groups differ. These are useful sources for comparison. They do not establish that a Minnesota staff member may override Nora’s relevant, voluntarily stated description.

Lee can preserve Nora’s and Evan’s different self-descriptions in the optional profiles, subject to the actual editorial and permission arrangements. There is no need to turn the profiles into a vote on which person understands disability correctly. Lee also should not infer that Nora rejects healthcare, that Evan rejects disability identity, or that either person uses a particular communication method. Those claims are not supplied by word order.

The learning question is how a description works, not how to classify a person. You may notice privately that one pattern feels more familiar to you. That observation can support curiosity about the other pattern without asking anyone to disclose a history. Use the invented profiles for practice; no personal information needs to be entered or shared.

flashcards.back: A wording pattern that mentions the person before a disability or condition. It does not tell the whole story of the person’s identity.
A wording pattern that names a disability-related identity as a description of the person. Its personal meaning is not established by the pattern alone.
A person’s choice of wording in a relevant context, when actually shared. It is not a clinical finding or a group-wide rule.
A conclusion added beyond what was said or observed. A preferred label does not establish healthcare views, support needs or ability.

items.title: Why two different descriptions can both be meaningful
items.body: Nora’s description may connect disability with a valued identity, while Evan’s may place the condition alongside other parts of his life. The practice case supplies their chosen words, not all their reasons. Respecting both does not require inventing contrasting personal philosophies or deciding which person has made greater progress.

items.title: What a style guide can and cannot do
items.body: A guide can explain a pattern and help an editor make a provisional choice when preference is unknown. It does not know every individual’s meaning or the permission governing a particular profile. Use guidance with the actual task rather than treating a general recommendation as authority to rewrite a person’s self-description.

items.title: Why word order does not establish support needs
items.body: A description concerns how someone is named or described. A meeting aid concerns how a person receives and conveys information in that task. Inferring the second from the first can bypass the person and miss a practical need. Keep those questions separate even when both arise in one interaction.

tabs.label: One pattern required for everyone
tabs.body: Lee could change both profiles to the same pattern to make them visually consistent. That produces uniform wording but removes a difference the contributors actually chose. The edit would need a legitimate reason under the real profile arrangement, rather than an assumption that one description is always disrespectful. Consistency is an editorial consideration; it is not evidence that every person attaches the same meaning to disability.

tabs.label: Different descriptions with personal choice
tabs.body: Lee can keep each relevant self-description while checking the ordinary editing and publication permission. This preserves what Nora and Evan contributed without requiring a debate about their identity. It also leaves unanswered questions honestly unanswered: neither profile establishes the person’s communication method, the relevance of disability in another task, or permission to disclose it elsewhere.

tabs.label: Language used to diagnose beliefs
tabs.body: Lee might infer that Nora is politically confident and Evan avoids disability identity. The profiles do not establish either claim. That interpretation changes an editing task into an unsupported personal judgment. Describe the pattern accurately, and ask a relevant, optional clarification only if the task needs one. The person need not defend the wording through a biography.

check.question: Which conclusion is supported by the practice profiles?
check.correct: Nora and Evan used different wording patterns; the descriptions do not establish their full beliefs or support needs.
wrong: Identity-first wording proves Nora does not want medical care.
Person-first wording proves Evan is uncomfortable with disability.
One pattern must be imposed on both contributors before either profile is respectful.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion describes what is present without assigning unprovided beliefs.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Nora’s word order does not establish a view about care. Evan’s description does not reveal discomfort with identity. Requiring one pattern treats editorial uniformity as proof of respect and ignores the relevant choices the case actually supplies. Recognize both patterns without turning them into a diagnosis or hierarchy.

A person with a disability
An autistic researcher
A disabled artist describing their chosen identity
A preferred term proves which aid someone needs.
An identity-first description reveals every healthcare preference.

responses: The general pattern does not invalidate Nora’s chosen description.
This respects the supplied wording without inferring broader beliefs or permission.

lessons.transfer: Privately compare the invented profiles, or reflect on a description you voluntarily use for yourself. Notice the wording and what it leaves unknown; no personal information needs to be recorded.

move.control: Describe the wording before interpreting the person.
move.failure: A familiar editorial pattern becomes an unsupported account of someone’s beliefs or needs.
move.next: Practice distinguishing the two descriptions in the practice case, at a pace you choose.

lessons.title: Invite a preference without making disclosure a condition
lessons.summary: Ask a brief, relevant question and respect a decision not to discuss identity.
lessons.objective: Choose a relevant and optional way to ask about a description.
objectives: Choose a relevant and optional way to ask about a description.
Distinguish an invitation about wording from a request for private information.
Respond appropriately when a practice contributor declines a disability description.
takeaways: Ask about the description needed for the actual task, rather than seeking a personal history.
A person may decline a disability label or an explanation.
Permission in one conversation does not establish permission to publish or reuse a description.
lessons.statement: Make the question useful and optional, and respect the limit of the answer.

image.caption: Three colleagues, one using a wheelchair, meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks.

intro.heading: Invite a preference without making disclosure a condition
intro.body:
Lee is preparing another optional contributor profile. Quinn has supplied a name, role and research interest, with no disability description. Lee wonders whether the profile should include one because other profiles do. This is a point at which an apparently inclusive question could become pressure. The profile’s purpose is to introduce contributors, not to require each person to identify a disability.

A relevant invitation might be, “Would you like any particular wording used in this profile? You can keep the description as it is.” That lets Quinn discuss the actual text without being asked to confirm a condition or explain identity. If a person has already chosen a disability description and clarification is needed, Lee can ask which wording they want in this specific profile. Neither question requires an account of diagnosis, treatment, discrimination or personal beliefs.

Quinn says, “Please just use my role and interests.” That is enough for this optional profile. Lee can accept the answer and continue the ordinary editing process. Declining a disability description is not evidence of shame, denial or a lack of solidarity. Quinn might have many reasons, or might simply prefer the shorter profile. The task does not require Lee to discover why.

Context matters as much as wording. A person might use a disability identity in a private conversation but not want it in an event biography. An answer about one profile does not automatically authorize a later publicity campaign, shared staff directory or account of someone’s health. Use the actual permission and information-handling arrangements; do not make this course an informal consent rule for every type of record.

The same care applies to who asks and where. A public request to declare a disability could create an unnecessary disclosure situation. A task-focused, optional clarification can often be handled with less exposure when it is actually needed. These are suggested communication choices for the practice example, not instructions to collect identity data from staff. Learning can be personal and unrecorded: notice how you distinguish interest in someone’s wording from a belief that you are entitled to the explanation.

flashcards.back: A question connected to the description or task at hand, rather than a general demand to explain identity.
A genuine opportunity to contribute or decline without making the answer a condition of participation in the invented activity.
The particular conversation, audience and use. A private description and a public profile are not automatically interchangeable.
The limits of the actual agreed use and applicable information handling. This course does not invent a universal consent procedure.

items.title: Why asking can become pressure
items.body: A question can sound friendly while making a person responsible for correcting the organization or revealing private information. Lee reduces that burden by making the optional profile’s purpose clear and offering a valid way to keep the supplied description. The person can contribute language without becoming a spokesperson for a group.

items.title: What to do with a declined explanation
items.body: Quinn’s answer gives Lee a usable editing direction: retain the role and interests. Asking repeatedly why Quinn will not disclose would not improve that decision. Accept the limit, avoid assigning a motive, and use the actual process if a different task genuinely requires information.

items.title: Why an audience change matters
items.body: A contributor may be comfortable using an identity in a chosen discussion but not in searchable publicity. The words alone do not settle reuse. Before moving material to another setting, check the real permission and information-handling requirements rather than treating familiarity with the person as a substitute.

tabs.label: Ask about the text
tabs.body: Lee asks which wording Quinn wants in this optional profile and offers to retain the existing description. The answer can directly guide the edit. This approach does not require Quinn to identify a disability or explain a private history. A brief clarification serves the communication task while leaving the contributor’s wider identity and reasons under their own control.

tabs.label: Ask for a biography to justify a term
tabs.body: Lee asks for diagnosis and past experiences so the editor can decide whether a preferred term is reasonable. That expands the task without an established need or proper information process. It also shifts authority over self-description to the editor. In the invented profile activity, a relevant wording choice can be understood without requiring medical evidence or a personal explanation.

tabs.label: Interpret a decline
tabs.body: Lee keeps pressing because a missing disability description seems less inclusive. That treats Quinn’s silence as a problem to solve and substitutes the editor’s meaning for the contributor’s stated choice. A profile can introduce Quinn through role and interests. The absence of a label does not establish the absence of disability, pride, trust or willingness to contribute.

check.question: Quinn wants the optional profile to include only role and interests. What is the supported next step?
check.correct: Use that description within the actual editing arrangement, without demanding a disability label or a reason for declining one.
wrong: Keep asking until Quinn explains the disability history.
Infer that Quinn is ashamed and add a disability description to help.
Publish a private identity description from an earlier conversation without checking the actual permission.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response uses the information Quinn chose to provide for this task.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Repeated questions turn an optional invitation into pressure. Adding a label based on presumed shame invents both a motive and a description. Reusing a private conversation assumes publication permission that has not been established. Respect the present task and the actual limits of the supplied information.

items.text: Which wording would you like in this optional profile?
Do you want us to keep the description you supplied?
Please use only my role and interests.
I do not want to discuss a disability description here.
Prove your diagnosis before choosing a profile term.
A missing label means the person is ashamed.

Treat earlier private wording as permission for all publicity.

responses: This respects the present description and does not invent reuse permission.
A past conversation does not establish every later audience or use.
The profile does not require a public account of Quinn’s reasons.

lessons.transfer: Privately draft a brief invitation for the invented profile, including a real option to keep the current text. Do not collect anyone’s disability information for this activity.

move.control: Ask only what the actual wording task needs.
move.failure: Interest in identity becomes repeated pressure to disclose or explain.
move.next: Use the practice exchange or private reflection to practice accepting a clear limit.

lessons.title: Choose relevant and precise descriptions
lessons.summary: Describe the person or task without adding pity, praise or unsupported limitations.
lessons.objective: Identify when disability is relevant to a practice description.
objectives: Identify when disability is relevant to a practice description.
Replace an unsupported limitation with a precise description of an observed task.
Distinguish a preferred term from an assumption about ability or communication.
takeaways: A description should serve the actual purpose rather than add an unnecessary label.
Pity or praise can introduce a story that the facts do not support.
A term does not establish a person’s contribution, communication method or required support.
lessons.statement: Describe what is relevant and known, and leave unsupported stories out.

image.caption: Three colleagues, one using a wheelchair, meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks.

intro.heading: Choose relevant and precise descriptions
intro.body:
Lee is editing a practice event announcement. One sentence says that Evan will discuss research on community participation. Another draft describes Evan as “confined to a wheelchair” and says that contributing to the event is courageous. Evan has supplied his research topic and chosen person-first description, but has not supplied that account of his experience. Lee must examine what the added language does.

An equipment description is not the same as a limitation on the whole person. A wheelchair can be described as a device someone uses when that fact is relevant and known. The word confined adds an interpretation about restriction. Likewise, routine participation does not establish that a person is overcoming disability or providing inspiration. Praise may be intended warmly, yet the draft still needs a basis for the particular claim. Lee can introduce Evan through the research contribution instead of inventing a personal struggle.

Relevance is a separate question from which disability term is preferred. If the announcement’s purpose is to identify the topic and speaker, disability might not need to be mentioned. If an approved first-person contribution discusses disability identity, the description may be relevant in that context. Neither choice should be made automatically from appearance, equipment or a staff member’s interest in creating an uplifting story.

Precision also matters when describing a task difficulty. “The file’s table did not work with the method used to read it” identifies a possible document issue to examine. “The contributor cannot understand research” makes a broad ability claim that the observation does not support. The course does not decide whether the document met a formal accessibility requirement; it shows why the narrower description leaves room for investigation and a practical response.

DOJ’s effective-communication guidance considers the actual communication and a person’s methods, rather than assuming one solution for everyone with a disability. That is a different question from whether the profile uses identity-first or person-first wording. A preferred description cannot tell Lee that Evan wants an interpreter, that Nora needs a particular format, or that Quinn has no access needs. Describe language accurately, and address a current practical need through the actual task and applicable process.

flashcards.back: A connection between a description and the purpose of the communication. Appearance alone does not make disability relevant.
A description limited to what is actually known or observed, rather than a broader account of ability or motive.
An uplifting claim added without evidence or the person’s account. A positive tone does not make the claim accurate.
The communication to be accomplished and how the person receives or conveys it. A disability label does not settle these questions.

items.title: Why a mobility device does not tell a life story
items.body: The invented draft supplies a wheelchair reference but no account of restriction or personal struggle. Describing use, when relevant, is more precise than assigning confinement. The difference is not a promise that the person faces no barriers; it keeps the editor from claiming knowledge the task does not provide.

items.title: Why praise should have a basis
items.body: Describing a specific research contribution can acknowledge useful work. Calling ordinary participation courageous only because of disability changes the focus to an unprovided personal narrative. Check what the contributor actually supplied and what the communication needs, rather than assuming admiration cannot carry a stereotype.

items.title: Why a narrower problem description helps
items.body: An unusable table and a presumed inability to understand are different explanations. The first directs attention to the document and task; the second may exclude the contributor without testing the actual difficulty. Precision supports a useful next inquiry while leaving formal accessibility decisions with their responsible process.

tabs.label: Role and contribution
tabs.body: The announcement names Evan’s research topic and the contribution he chose to discuss. Readers learn why the presentation is relevant without an unsupported story about his body or life. If disability identity is relevant to the supplied contribution, it can be addressed through that content and its actual editing agreement, rather than automatically added to every introduction.

tabs.label: Pity as description
tabs.body: The draft calls Evan confined and presents attendance as overcoming a personal limitation. Those claims go beyond the supplied information. Removing them does not deny that barriers may exist; it distinguishes a possible barrier from a story the editor invented. The contributor’s role and actual account provide a stronger basis for the announcement.

tabs.label: A broad ability conclusion
tabs.body: An editor treats a file-reading difficulty as proof that Nora cannot follow the research. That skips the actual file, communication method and task. A precise description keeps the practical question open: what information must be received and conveyed, and what is not working? A preferred identity label neither answers nor removes that question.

check.question: Which edit best fits the practice announcement?
check.correct: Introduce Evan’s research contribution and use a relevant, accurate description rather than adding an unprovided story of confinement or courage.
wrong: Keep the confinement claim because it sounds sympathetic.
Add a claim of bravery because positive language is always accurate.
Infer Nora’s comprehension from a difficulty using one file.
check.feedbackCorrect: The edit matches the purpose and the information actually supplied.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Sympathy does not establish confinement. A positive claim still needs a basis and can assign an unwanted narrative. A difficulty with a file does not prove broad comprehension limits. Keep the description specific, and examine any actual communication difficulty separately.

items.text: Evan supplied a research topic for the event announcement.
The contributor has chosen wording for the approved profile.
Is disability relevant to this announcement’s purpose?
What about this table is not working with the communication method used?
Using a wheelchair proves the person is confined.
Ordinary attendance proves the person overcame disability.

lessons.transfer: Use the invented announcement to compare an observed fact with an added story. You may reflect privately on how praise or sympathy affects your editing; no actual person needs to be described.

lessons.title: Apply editorial guidance while preserving voice
lessons.summary: Distinguish general wording, chosen self-description and exact source language.
lessons.objective: Compare a general editorial recommendation with a contributor’s relevant self-description.
objectives: Compare a general editorial recommendation with a contributor’s relevant self-description.
Distinguish an editable paraphrase from an exact quotation or legal term.
Choose an appropriate next step when wording and record requirements appear to conflict.
takeaways: General guidance helps with unknown preference but does not know every individual.
Quotations and legally significant terms require accuracy and the actual editing process.
A language exercise does not authorize rewriting a record or changing a program definition.
lessons.statement: Fit the wording to the purpose while preserving accuracy and actual authority.

image.caption: Three colleagues, one using a wheelchair, meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks.

intro.heading: Apply editorial guidance while preserving voice
intro.body:
Lee now has three different editing tasks. The first is a general event paragraph about disability participation. The second is Nora’s optional self-description. The third is a reference to wording in a historical source. Using one automatic replacement for all three would miss important differences. The paragraph, the profile and the quotation have different relationships to the writer’s voice and to accuracy.

General editorial guidance is useful when a communication describes a broad audience and no individual preference is available. NIH and CDC provide recommendations and acknowledge differing usage. Lee can consult the actual editorial arrangements and the intended audience rather than claim that the course establishes a universal DHS style rule. A general choice can be provisional and open to relevant feedback. It should not be turned into a claim that every reader agrees.

Nora’s self-description carries a different kind of information: an actual contributor has supplied wording for a particular use. An editor can discuss clarity or an applicable requirement without silently replacing that choice because another pattern feels more familiar. If a real conflict arises, use the responsible editorial process and explain the specific issue. Do not ask the contributor to defend an identity through medical documentation.

A quotation or legally significant term also requires care. Rewriting the words inside an exact quotation can make the source inaccurate. A historical term may need relevant context instead of being presented as the program’s preferred description. Likewise, staff cannot change an eligibility definition or official data category simply by applying a language exercise. Appropriate explanation, a clearly identified paraphrase or an authorized revision may be possible, depending on the actual task and authority.

The goal is thoughtful judgment, not endless hesitation. Lee can identify which type of text is being edited, what can be changed, who supplied the wording and which actual process governs the work. That creates a useful next step without assuming that one spelling or word order resolves every issue. Optional practice can remain practice: compare the three tasks and explain a choice privately without opening or changing an actual record.

flashcards.back: Recommendations for a communication context. They can inform a provisional choice without proving unanimous preference.
Words a person supplies about themself for a particular purpose. Relevant choice and actual reuse permission are separate considerations.
An identified reproduction of another source’s words. An unmarked rewrite can misrepresent what the source said.
A change made through the actual responsible process and authority. A course exercise does not confer that authority.

items.title: How to use a provisional choice
items.body: A writer may need language before every preference is known. Use relevant guidance and actual editorial arrangements, avoid claiming that all people agree, and remain open to appropriate feedback. The provisional choice helps complete the communication; it does not establish a permanent description for every person.

items.title: How to handle a source with outdated terms
items.body: Preserve the accuracy of a necessary quotation and explain its historical context where useful. A clearly identified paraphrase is different from silently changing quoted words. Decide what the task truly needs and use the real review arrangement; do not reproduce harmful wording merely to provide a language exercise.

items.title: What to do when a definition cannot be edited casually
items.body: A program definition or official category may have consequences beyond the sentence. A clearer explanatory phrase can be proposed through the appropriate process, but a staff writer should not silently change eligibility meaning or recode data. Respectful copy and accurate administration must be considered together.

tabs.label: General paragraph
tabs.body: Lee needs a workable description for a broad event paragraph. Relevant editorial guidance can help when no personal preference applies, and audience input can improve the wording. The choice is not evidence that every person has the same identity preference. A general paragraph can be clear without pretending it speaks for all readers or imposing its style on their own descriptions.

tabs.label: Contributor’s chosen voice
tabs.body: Nora supplied a self-description for the optional profile. That is concrete information the general paragraph lacks. Lee can preserve it within the actual agreement and discuss any specific editorial issue directly. Automatically replacing it would use a broad recommendation to erase a relevant choice. Respect for voice does not eliminate ordinary accuracy or permission requirements.

tabs.label: Quotation or defined term
tabs.body: A historical quotation or official definition must remain accurately represented. Lee can consider a necessary quotation’s context, a clearly identified paraphrase or a proposed authorized revision. Silently changing the source or a consequential definition is a different action from improving ordinary copy. The lesson does not grant permission to alter records or program meaning.

check.question: Which approach best fits the three practice editing tasks?
check.correct: Distinguish general copy, a supplied self-description and exact source wording, then use the actual guidance, permission and authority relevant to each.
wrong: Run one automatic replacement across profiles, quotations and program definitions.
Treat a general recommendation as proof that every contributor prefers the same words.
Change a legal definition privately because the revised wording feels more respectful.
check.feedbackCorrect: Different text functions require different editing judgments.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Automatic replacement can erase chosen voice or misquote a source. A recommendation does not establish unanimous preference. A consequential definition requires its actual authority and process, not an informal change of meaning. Identify the task before choosing the edit.

items.text: Consult the actual style arrangement for a broad event paragraph.
Consider relevant audience feedback without claiming everyone agrees.
Keep an exact quotation accurate and provide relevant context.
Clarify a contributor’s supplied description within the actual editing agreement.
Replace words inside every quotation without identifying the change.
Privately revise eligibility meaning through a language exercise.

Ask one contributor to decide every program definition.
responses: Consistency alone does not protect voice, quotation accuracy or consequential definitions.
This identifies the appropriate judgment instead of assuming one action fits every text.
A contributor’s preference does not confer authority over all definitions.

move.failure: One helpful recommendation becomes an automatic change across different kinds of text.
move.next: Use the practice tasks to practice accuracy, choice and appropriate review at your own pace.

lessons.title: Respond to a correction without asking for reassurance
lessons.summary: Make a useful wording repair while recognizing a separate concern or formal responsibility.
lessons.objective: Choose a brief, task-focused response to a practice wording correction.
objectives: Choose a brief, task-focused response to a practice wording correction.
Distinguish an ordinary editing repair from a protected-class concern.
Identify the immediate manager reporting responsibility under Policy 1436 without deciding a case.
takeaways: A correction can guide a useful repair without requiring a long defense of intent.
A person does not owe reassurance, a personal history or agreement that the issue is resolved.

lessons.statement: Use the correction to improve the interaction and retain any separate responsibility.

image.caption: Three colleagues, one using a wheelchair, meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks.

intro.heading: Respond to a correction without asking for reassurance
intro.body:
Lee accidentally changes Nora’s supplied identity-first description. Nora replies, “Please use the wording I gave you.” Lee could explain the edit at length, ask Nora to confirm that no offense was taken, or make the relevant correction. In this practice profile task, a brief acknowledgement and the agreed repair are useful: “Thank you for pointing that out. I’ll restore your wording in this draft.” The next question is whether the correction is actually made within the editing arrangement, not whether Nora supplies emotional reassurance.

An explanation of intent can sometimes be relevant, but it should not displace the person’s clear editing request. Lee does not need to defend an entire character or ask Nora to teach a general course on disability. Nor should the editor require Nora to share more personal information before restoring words already supplied for the profile. A calm response keeps attention on the task and leaves the contributor free to move on.

A more serious concern requires a different response as well. In another practice exchange, a supervisor learns of alleged repeated disability-related mockery in the team. That is not merely a dispute about whether a biography uses one word order. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow the actual agency complaint and investigation procedures. An apology, training suggestion or informal discussion cannot replace or delay that responsibility. This course makes no finding about a live allegation.

Employees are strongly encouraged under that policy to report incidents through its available routes. The course does not assert that every learner has the identical manager duty or that someone must first confront the person involved. Actual assigned investigation responsibilities remain with the applicable procedures and authority; avoid an improvised inquiry outside those roles. Respectful communication and formal response can both be necessary.

Finally, a correction does not prove that all effects have been repaired. Lee can confirm the revised draft and address any known next step without asking Nora to certify trust or forgive the interaction. Learning from a mistake can be worthwhile even if no visible outcome follows. You can practice the exchange privately with the example, without reproducing an actual complaint or identifying a colleague.

flashcards.back: A brief recognition of the information or correction received. It need not become a request for reassurance.
A relevant action within the actual task and authority, such as restoring agreed profile wording.
An allegation or incident requiring the actual applicable reporting and complaint process, rather than an informal language exercise.
Responsibility under the actual agency procedures. This course neither grants investigation authority nor cancels duties assigned through those procedures.

items.title: Why a short response can be useful
items.body: Nora has supplied a clear request about the draft. Lee can acknowledge it and restore the agreed wording without asking Nora to judge the editor’s intention. A short response is not avoidance when it is followed by the relevant action. It keeps the task from becoming another burden for the contributor.

items.title: Why informal repair and formal response can coexist
items.body: An editor can correct a sentence while an actual protected-class concern follows the appropriate process. These actions address different questions. For a manager or supervisor, the required immediate report cannot wait for a team discussion to succeed, an apology to be accepted or a course to be completed.

items.title: Why a person’s response is not a closure certificate
items.body: Nora may say little after the edit, or may have concerns beyond the profile. Neither silence nor thanks establishes that trust has been restored. Confirm the action that is actually known and keep any relevant responsibility visible. Avoid assigning a positive outcome merely because the interaction ended politely.

tabs.label: Defend intention
tabs.body: Lee spends the reply explaining that the edit was meant to be respectful and asks Nora to confirm that the editor is a good colleague. That may make Nora responsible for the editor’s comfort instead of completing the requested repair. Intent can be considered without using it to deny the clear wording request or requiring reassurance before restoring the draft.

tabs.label: Acknowledge and act
tabs.body: Lee thanks Nora for the correction and restores the supplied description within the actual profile arrangement. This is a specific, checkable action. It does not claim that every impact is resolved or that no further concern can exist. The reply leaves room for Nora’s choice while returning attention to the agreed task.

tabs.label: Keep a serious concern in its proper process
tabs.body: The supervisor receives an allegation of disability-related mockery. A respectful conversation may still be useful, but the supervisor immediately reports under Policy 1436 to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follows agency procedures. The process is not conditional on the employee accepting an apology or trying informal confrontation first.

check.question: In this example, a supervisor learns of alleged disability-related mockery. Which response preserves the applicable responsibility?
check.correct: Immediately report the allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow actual agency procedures, while handling any appropriate wording repair separately.
wrong: Wait to see whether a training session solves the problem.
Require the employee to confront the person first.
Conduct an improvised private investigation outside assigned agency procedures and authority.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response retains the manager reporting duty and the actual formal process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Training cannot delay the supervisor’s immediate report. The policy does not make direct confrontation a prerequisite to reporting. An improvised investigation can exceed the role and procedure; preserve any investigation duties actually assigned under agency procedures instead. A language course neither finds a violation nor replaces the process.

lessons.statement: Follow through on what is known and keep different needs distinct.

image.caption: Three colleagues, one using a wheelchair, meet at a white table with laptops and notebooks.

intro.heading: Carry language choices into thoughtful follow-through
intro.body:
The practice profiles are nearly ready. Nora’s description has been restored, Evan’s research contribution is accurately introduced, and Quinn’s profile contains only the chosen role and interests. Lee has completed several useful editing actions. It would still be inaccurate to conclude that the event is fully accessible, that every contributor trusts the organizers, or that no further response is needed. Those questions require different information.

A description preference concerns how someone is named or described in this context. A communication need concerns receiving and conveying information in a task. An actual record or decision concerns what the responsible process permits or requires. They can arise together, but one does not answer all the others. Nora’s identity-first wording does not select a meeting format. Quinn’s missing disability label does not establish an absence of needs. A correctly edited profile does not demonstrate that a separate registration document can be used.

Lee can make a task-focused inquiry when appropriate: confirm the agreed profile text and use the actual arrangements for any communication request that arises. In state employment, Policy 1433 recognizes initial accommodation requests without special words; subsequent documentation, decision roles and information handling still apply. The recipient promptly forwards the request to the appropriate decision maker and identifies that decision maker to the requestor. Supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation; appropriate requests belong to the ADA Coordinator. A language conversation is not a reason to improvise those roles.

For service communication, DOJ guidance examines the actual task and the person’s communication method. Public entities give primary consideration to requested aids under the applicable requirements and qualifications. A staff member does not select an aid or declare an exception merely from a disability label. The course’s practice profile activity is not a legal test of effective communication or formal accommodation approval.

The learning can also change how Lee understands a personal interaction outside a workplace task. Recognizing that a preferred term has meaning without explaining a whole person is a worthwhile insight. You can keep that reflection private and unrecorded. There is no requirement to collect a colleague’s preference, produce a live document or prove a lasting change. If actual work is undertaken, retain its relevant permission, review, analysis and formal responsibilities rather than treating completion of this optional course as sufficient.

inThisLesson: Distinguish wording preference, communication access and evidence of a completed action.
Choose a proportionate follow-through step in a practice contributor interaction.
Explain a private learning insight without claiming compliance or a lasting outcome.
Which follow-through is best supported?
lessons.keyStatement: Follow through on what is known and keep different needs distinct.

flashcards.back: Wording a person chooses for a relevant context. It does not determine every communication method or authorize every later use.
What is needed to receive and convey information in the actual task. Ask and respond through applicable arrangements rather than a label-based assumption.
A specific step that can be accurately described, such as restoring supplied wording. It is not proof of every desired outcome.
Personal understanding that can be valuable without recording, disclosing identity or submitting a live work product.

items.title: How to follow through without collecting a new identity list
items.body: Lee can use the agreed profile text for its actual purpose and handle an appropriate new request when it arises. This does not require creating a permanent directory of disability identities. Actual information handling, permission and reuse requirements apply to real work; course practice should use the invented cases rather than staff information.

items.title: How to avoid confusing a term with an access plan
items.body: A disability description does not establish that someone reads Braille, uses sign language or wants a particular format. Examine the communication and the person’s methods through the responsible arrangement. A respectful introduction can be retained while a practical access problem is addressed; neither should be treated as proof that the other is unnecessary.

items.title: How to describe learning honestly
items.body: Lee can say that the profile wording was restored, while any wider effects remain unknown. A learner can say that comparing descriptions prompted a private insight. Neither statement certifies formal compliance or predicts enduring trust. Accurate descriptions of limited progress allow useful learning without exaggerated claims.

tabs.label: Wording as the whole solution
tabs.body: Lee could treat the corrected profiles as proof that all access concerns are settled. That conclusion reaches beyond the edits. Contributors still need to receive and convey information in the actual event, and other materials may have separate issues. A respectful term is worthwhile without making it evidence about every feature or experience of the program.

tabs.label: Connected but distinct follow-through
tabs.body: Lee confirms the agreed text and directs any actual communication or accommodation request through the relevant arrangements. This keeps the language choice useful while preserving the separate task, method, authority and privacy questions. It avoids diagnosing a need from a label or requiring a person to debate identity before an appropriate response can begin.

tabs.label: A private learning insight
tabs.body: A learner may recognize a habit of treating preferred words as clues to a person’s entire worldview. That insight can support a more careful personal interaction even without a work document. Private, unrecorded reflection is a valid way to learn. It does not need to be converted into an identity disclosure, staff survey or claim that the learner has certified a live process.

check.question: Which conclusion accurately describes the practice follow-through?
check.correct: The relevant profile edits are completed; communication needs, formal requirements and wider effects remain separate questions to address when applicable.
wrong: Correct profile wording proves the entire event is accessible.
Quinn’s omitted disability description proves no communication support could be needed.
Completing this optional course replaces the actual DHS equity analysis or accommodation process.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion names completed actions without making unsupported claims about other needs or requirements.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An edited profile does not test every event feature. A missing identity label does not establish the absence of communication needs. Optional learning cannot replace applicable formal tools, analysis, decision roles or accommodation requirements. Preserve the value of the edits while keeping each remaining question honest.

items.text: Nora’s supplied wording was restored in the approved draft.
A learner privately notices an assumption about identity labels.
What communication method is needed for the actual event task?
Which real information-handling and decision requirements apply?
A correct term certifies the whole event’s access.
A missing disability label proves no support need exists.

lessons.next: Continue with a private insight or an appropriate next step for a suitable draft.

options: Confirm the agreed edits and address the actual format question through the relevant arrangements without inferring everyone’s needs from identity wording.

responses: This connects wording with practical response while retaining separate roles and requirements.
The profile wording does not establish the document’s usability or every person’s experience.
A general disclosure demand is not created by this course or this practice profile activity.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice case to name one completed edit and one separate question, or keep a personal insight private and unrecorded. Do not gather identity or accommodation information as a course exercise.

move.control: Describe a limited action accurately and preserve separate needs and responsibilities.
move.failure: A respectful term becomes proof of complete access, compliance or trust.
move.next: At your own pace, retain a private insight or consider an appropriate next step for a practice case or suitable draft.

jobAid.subtitle: A short aid for respectful, accurate disability descriptions.
remember: Understand person-first and identity-first patterns without ranking the people who use them.
A relevant preference, actual publication permission and a communication need are different questions.
Private learning is valid; do not collect disability information for course practice.

sections.heading: Choose the description thoughtfully
items: Identify the actual purpose and whether disability is relevant.
Use a relevant, voluntarily supplied preference within the actual editing and permission arrangements.
When preference is unknown, use appropriate guidance without claiming unanimous agreement.
Avoid inferring ability, beliefs or support needs from wording or appearance.

sections.heading: Protect accuracy and choice
items: Ask a brief, task-focused and genuinely optional clarification when needed.
Respect a decision to omit a disability description from an optional profile.
Distinguish general copy, self-description, quotation and consequential defined terms.
Do not silently rewrite quotations, legal meaning or official records through a language exercise.

sections.heading: Respond and follow through
items: Acknowledge a correction and make the relevant repair without demanding reassurance.
Keep actual communication and employment-accommodation requests in their proper processes.
Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures.
Describe a completed step without claiming every effect is resolved or formal requirements are fulfilled.

sources.title: NIH: Person-first and destigmatizing language

sources.title: CDC: Preferred terms for population groups and communities
sources.note: The disability section acknowledges identity-first preference, differing views within groups and context-sensitive wording. This is communication guidance, not a rule that overrides a person’s expressed preference.

sources.title: DOJ: Effective communication
sources.note: Actual communication methods and the task’s context are separate from the words used to describe disability. Public-entity primary consideration has applicable legal qualifications; the course does not authorize an exception.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: Reasonable accommodation
sources.note: Initial employment-accommodation requests do not require special words. Actual processing, decision roles and privacy requirements remain applicable; a wording conversation does not substitute for them.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Actual reporting and agency complaint procedures remain separate. Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Equity expectations apply to relevant daily practices and decisions. An optional language exercise does not replace required analysis, tools or authorized decisions.
